destination.title: The phone in his pocket testified against him for months

short08: Your phone keeps a record of everywhere you go.
Police wanted a hundred and twenty-seven days of it, without a warrant.
Every few minutes, a phone connects to a nearby cell tower and leaves a trace of where you are.
Police got months of that location history from the carrier, and placed a suspect near a string of robberies.
In 2018, the Supreme Court said no.
This much location data needs a warrant.
For the first time, your digital trail was protected.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: In 2011, police used 127 days of one man's location records to place him near a string of robberies — and they got those records without a warrant .
And the police had gathered that 127-day map without a warrant .
In 2010 and 2011, a series of armed robberies hit stores around Detroit, Michigan — electronics shops and phone stores, hit by a rotating crew .
They went to his wireless carriers and asked for something most people in 2011 did not know existed: his cell-site location information .
The government obtained around 127 days of Carpenter's records — almost 13,000 location points, about 12,898 in all, tracing where his phone had been .
He was convicted and sentenced to 116 years in prison .
The reason they were allowed to do that came from a rule almost no one outside a courtroom had ever heard of.
The government could get it without a warrant, because, in the eyes of the law, it was no longer really yours .
In 1979, applied to a list of dialed phone numbers, that idea was already aggressive, but it was containable .
In 2018, by a vote of five to four, the Supreme Court ruled for Carpenter .
This was not a single trip or a single call.
A blurry line invites years of new cases just to find where it really falls — and until they are decided, no one is quite sure .
It did not say the government can never see your data.
era_note: SET THIS. Modern stock footage is only usable if the case is modern; a 1960s case dressed in present-day footage reads wrong.

shorts.angle: The reason nobody needed a warrant for Timothy Carpenter's twelve thousand location points was a rule from the 1970s that said anything you hand to a company stops being yours.
shorts.type: B — a number/stakes gap (12,898 points, 116 years, no warrant)
shorts.avoids: The existing Short states the 127 days and the 2018 outcome. It never gives the size of the map, the sentence he was serving, or the name of the doctrine that made the whole thing legal in the first place.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: What the third-party doctrine says about every other record a company holds about you, and whether the Court touched it.
shorts.loop_join: L5 ends on an instruction to count, and L1 supplies the number, so the doctrine and its price tag read as one continuous thought.

shorts.angle: Carpenter was five to four, and the four who lost warned that the majority had swapped a clear rule for a blurry line nobody could locate, which the majority admitted and took anyway.

shorts.avoids: The existing Short ends on 'for the first time, your digital trail was protected'. It never says the ruling was contested, that the Court refused to overturn the old doctrine rather than replacing it, or that four justices predicted years of uncertainty.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: Which of your other trails — searches, purchases, messages — the same logic reaches, and which it leaves exposed.

lines.text: Carpenter won five to four. The four who lost thought the Court had just made everything worse.
source_lines: In 2018, by a vote of five to four, the Supreme Court ruled for Carpenter
The four dissenting justices warned that the Court had opened a door it could not close

lines.text: The majority did not throw out the old rule. It refused to extend it. Location records were different, Roberts wrote. A comprehensive, effortless chronicle of a person's movements.
source_lines: The Court did not throw out the third-party doctrine. It refused to extend it
Cell-site location information, Roberts wrote, was a new kind of record — a comprehensive, detailed, effortless chronicle of a person's movements

lines.text: The dissenters warned the Court had opened a door it could not close. How much data is too much? They said it had traded a clear rule for a vague one.
source_lines: The four dissenting justices warned that the Court had opened a door it could not close
Where exactly is the line? How much data is too much?
They argued the Court had traded a clear rule for a vague one, and that drawing these lines was a job for legislatures, not judges

lines.text: And they had a point. A clear rule tells police exactly what they may do. A blurry line invites years of new cases just to find where it falls.
source_lines: A clear rule, even an uncomfortable one, tells the police exactly what they may do. A blurry line invites years of new cases just to find where it really falls

lines.text: Nobody on that Court thought the answer was easy. The margin says so, and so does what the dissenters wrote.
